Modify merge sort: while merging, every time you take an item from the **right** half, it's smaller than everything still waiting in the left half, so it forms one inversion with each of them (`left.len() - i` inversions at once). Have a recursive helper return both the sorted Vec and the count.
hints: Write `fn sort_and_count(v: &[i32]) -> (Vec<i32>, u64)`; the base case returns `(v.to_vec(), 0)`.
Sort and count both halves, add their counts, then merge. Taking from the left on ties (`<=`) keeps equal items from counting.
When you take `right[j]`, add `(left.len() - i) as u64` to the count: every item still left in `left` is bigger.

algorithms-5.task: Write `fn dedup_sorted(v: &mut Vec<i32>)` that removes repeated values from a **sorted** Vec in place, keeping one of each, with read and write pointers. No `dedup`, `retain`, `remove` or sets. The tests include 200,000 copies of the same value, where calling `remove` for each repeat would be O(n²).
hints: The first item is always kept, so start with `write = 1` (after handling an empty Vec).
For each `read` from 1: if `v[read]` differs from the last kept value `v[write - 1]`, copy it to `v[write]` and increase `write`.
Finish with `v.truncate(write);`

forbid.message: Use read and write indices, without `dedup`, `retain`, `remove` or a set.

algorithms-5.task:
A city builds a reservoir between two of the walls along a valley. `walls[i]` is the height of wall `i`, and walls are one unit apart. Water between walls `i < j` fills up to the lower wall: the amount is `min(walls[i], walls[j]) * (j - i)`. Write `fn max_water(walls: &[u32]) -> u64`: the most water any pair of walls can hold (0 with fewer than two walls).

Start with the two outermost walls. Then move the pointer at the **lower** wall inward: keeping the lower wall can never do better, because any pair using it is narrower and still limited by its height. The tests have 100,000 walls.
hints: Start with `i = 0`, `j = walls.len() - 1` and `best = 0`.
Each step: the water is `walls[i].min(walls[j]) as u64 * (j - i) as u64`; keep the maximum.
Then move the lower side: `if walls[i] < walls[j] { i += 1 } else { j -= 1 }`.
checkNames: two walls hold the lower height
wide low walls can beat narrow tall ones
fewer than two walls hold nothing

algorithms-6.task: A fundraiser wants the **shortest** run of consecutive days whose donations reach a target. Write `fn shortest_at_least(values: &[u32], target: u64) -> Option<usize>`: the length of the shortest window with a sum of at least `target`, or `None` if no window gets there. All values are non-negative, so a variable-size window works: grow it to the right, and while the sum is at least the target, record the length and shrink from the left. The tests have 200,000 values.
hints: Keep `left`, a running `sum: u64`, and `best: Option<usize>`.
After adding `values[right]`, loop `while sum >= target && left <= right`: the window `left..=right` qualifies, so record `right + 1 - left`, then remove `values[left]` and move `left` on.
`best = Some(best.map_or(len, |b| b.min(len)));` keeps the smallest length seen.
checkNames: returns none when the target is out of reach

algorithms-6.task:
The password checker wants the **longest run of characters without a repeat**. Write `fn longest_unique_run(text: &str) -> usize`, counting characters (not bytes). For `"abcabcbb"` it's 3 (`"abc"`); for `"pwwkew"` it's 3 (`"wke"`).

Slide a window over the characters and keep a `HashMap<char, usize>` of the position where each character was last seen. When the new character was last seen inside the window, move `left` just past that position. The tests include a 200,000-character text whose longest unique run is 20,000 characters, so restarting from every position is too slow.
hints: Loop over `text.chars().enumerate()`, so `right` counts characters.
If `last_seen.get(&c)` finds a position `prev` with `prev >= left`, the window already holds `c`: set `left = prev + 1`. (An older `prev` before `left` doesn't matter.)
Then `last_seen.insert(c, right);` and `best = best.max(right + 1 - left);`
checkNames: the run can be in the middle
ignores repeats from before the window

algorithms-7.task:
Find the **balance point** of a list of weights: the first index `i` where the total of everything to the left of `i` equals the total of everything to the right of `i` (the item at `i` itself counts for neither side). Write `fn balance_point(values: &[i64]) -> Option<usize>`. For `[1, 7, 3, 6, 5, 6]` it's 3 (1 + 7 + 3 = 11 = 5 + 6).

Compute the total once. Then walk the list with a running `left` sum: the right side is `total - left - values[i]`. That's O(n); recomputing both sides at every index is O(n²), and the tests have 200,001 values.
hints: `let total: i64 = values.iter().sum();` and `let mut left = 0;`
At index `i` the right side is `total - left - values[i]`. If it equals `left`, return `Some(i)`.
Otherwise add `values[i]` to `left` and move on. After the loop, `None`.
checkNames: returns none without a balance point

algorithms-7.task:
Finance wants to know how many runs of consecutive transactions net out to exactly `k` (for example, how many periods ended with no net change). Write `fn count_subarrays_with_sum(values: &[i64], k: i64) -> u64`. Values can be negative, so a sliding window won't do.

Walk the values with a running total and a `HashMap<i64, u64>` counting how often each prefix total has appeared, starting with the empty prefix (total 0, seen once). At each step, add the number of earlier prefixes equal to `total - k`, then record the current total. The tests include 100,000 values, where checking every range would be O(n²).
hints: Start the map with `seen.insert(0, 1);`: the empty prefix before any value.
For each value: `total += v;` then add `seen.get(&(total - k))` (if any) to the count.
Only then record the current prefix: `*seen.entry(total).or_insert(0) += 1;`
checkNames: counts nothing when no range matches

recursion-dp-1.task: Write `fn is_palindrome(chars: &[char]) -> bool` recursively with slice patterns, no loops: a slice with zero or one characters is a palindrome; a longer one is a palindrome if its first and last characters are equal **and** the middle part is a palindrome. The pattern `[first, middle @ .., last]` splits off both ends at once.
hints: `match chars { [] | [_] => true, ... }` covers the base cases.
`[first, middle @ .., last] => first == last && is_palindrome(middle)`

require.message: `is_palindrome` should call itself on the middle part.

forbid.message: Solve it with recursion and slice patterns, no loops or iterators.

recursion-dp-1.task:
**Fast exponentiation.** Hashing and cryptography need `base` to the power `exp`, modulo `m`, for exponents like 10^18. Multiplying `exp` times would take centuries. Recursion halves the exponent instead:

- `exp == 0`: the answer is `1 % m`
- otherwise compute `half = pow_mod(base, exp / 2, m)`; the answer is `half * half % m`, times one more `base % m` (then `% m`) if `exp` is odd

That's O(log exp) multiplications: about 60 for 10^18. Write `fn pow_mod(base: u64, exp: u64, m: u64) -> u64`. The modulus is between 1 and 1,000,000,007, so the product of two numbers below `m` fits in a `u64`. Reduce `base` with `% m` before multiplying, since it can be bigger than `m`.
hints: Base case: `if exp == 0 { return 1 % m; }` (`1 % m` makes the `m == 1` case come out as 0).
`let half = pow_mod(base, exp / 2, m); let square = half * half % m;`
If `exp % 2 == 1`, return `square * (base % m) % m`; otherwise `square`.

forbid.message: Halve the exponent recursively: no loops and no `.pow()`.

checkNames: anything to the zero is one

recursion-dp-2.task:
The coach picks teams of exactly `k` players. Write `fn team_options(players: &[&str], k: usize) -> Vec<String>` that lists every team, each written as the names joined with `+` in the players' order, with the teams in order too: for `["ana", "ben", "cy"]` and `k = 2` that's `["ana+ben", "ana+cy", "ben+cy"]`. `k` is at least 1; if it's bigger than the number of players, there are no teams.

Use backtracking with a `Vec<&str>` path: for each player from a start position, choose them, explore the rest, un-choose. Prune when there aren't enough players left to fill the team.
hints: Write a helper `fn pick<'a>(players: &[&'a str], start: usize, k: usize, team: &mut Vec<&'a str>, out: &mut Vec<String>)`.
When `team.len() == k`, push `team.join("+")` and return. Otherwise loop `i` from `start`: push `players[i]`, recurse with `i + 1`, pop.
Prune with `if players.len() - i < k - team.len() { break; }`: not enough players remain.
checkNames: a team of everyone has one option
too few players means no teams
counts teams of three from twenty

recursion-dp-2.task:
**The N-Queens puzzle**, a backtracking classic: place `n` queens on an `n` by `n` chessboard so that no two attack each other (no two share a row, a column or a diagonal). Write `fn n_queens(n: usize) -> usize` that counts the solutions. There are 92 for the standard 8 by 8 board.

Place one queen per row, recursively. Keep three `Vec<bool>` of "taken" markers: columns (`n`), diagonals going one way (`row + col`, `2n` of them) and the other way (`row + n - 1 - col`). For each column of the current row that is free on all three, mark, recurse into the next row, unmark. Reaching row `n` means you found a solution.
hints: Write a helper `place(n, row, cols, diag, anti) -> usize` that returns 1 when `row == n`.
In row `row`, a queen in column `col` uses diagonal `row + col` and anti-diagonal `row + n - 1 - col`. Skip the column if any of the three is taken.
Otherwise mark all three, add `place(n, row + 1, ...)` to the count, then unmark them (that's the un-choose).
checkNames: two and three have no solution

recursion-dp-3.task:
A delivery robot moves through a warehouse grid from the top-left cell to the bottom-right cell, only ever moving **right** or **down**. `#` cells are shelves it can't enter. Write `fn count_paths(grid: &[&str]) -> u64`: the number of different routes (0 if the start or the end is a shelf, or the grid is empty).

Recursively, the number of routes from cell `(r, c)` is the routes from the cell below plus the routes from the cell to the right; from the bottom-right cell it's 1. Memoize on the position with a `HashMap<(usize, usize), u64>`. The tests include an empty 18 by 18 grid, which has over two billion routes.
hints: Convert the rows to bytes first (`row.bytes().collect::<Vec<u8>>()`), so you can index `grid[r][c]`.
In a helper `routes(grid, r, c, memo)`: off the grid or on a `#` gives 0; the bottom-right cell gives 1; otherwise check the memo.
On a miss: `routes(grid, r + 1, c, memo) + routes(grid, r, c + 1, memo)`, insert it under `(r, c)`, return it.
checkNames: counts routes in an open grid
a blocked start or end has no routes
a single cell has one route
an empty grid has no routes

recursion-dp-3.task:
A search engine splits hashtags into words: can `"applepenapple"` be written as a sequence of dictionary words? Yes: apple + pen + apple. Write `fn can_segment(text: &str, words: &[&str]) -> bool` (words may be reused; an empty text can always be segmented).

Recursively: the text from position `start` can be segmented if some dictionary word matches at `start` and the rest (from `start + word.len()`) can be segmented. Without a memo, a text like `"aaaa...ab"` with the words `a`, `aa`, `aaa`, `aaaa` makes the recursion try an astronomical number of splits. Memoize on `start` with a `HashMap<usize, bool>`. Use `text[start..].starts_with(word)`. (The tests use ASCII text, so byte positions are fine.)
hints: Write a helper `from(text, start, words, memo) -> bool`: `start == text.len()` means everything was split, so `true`.
Check the memo for `start`. On a miss, try every word: if `text[start..].starts_with(w)` and `from(text, start + w.len(), words, memo)`, the answer is `true`.
Store the answer for `start` before returning it, whether it's `true` or `false` (remembering failures is what saves the time).
checkNames: rejects a text with a leftover
tries more than the first match
empty text can always be segmented
handles a long unsplittable text quickly

recursion-dp-4.task:
The vending machine team wants to know in how many **different ways** an amount can be paid (order doesn't matter: 1 + 2 and 2 + 1 are the same way). Write `fn ways_to_pay(coins: &[u32], amount: u32) -> u64`. There's 1 way to pay 0.

State: `ways[a]` = number of ways to pay `a` with the coins considered so far. Loop over the **coins on the outside** and the amounts on the inside: `ways[a] += ways[a - coin]`. (With the amounts outside you'd count 1 + 2 and 2 + 1 separately.) The tests include paying 10,000 with eight coin values.
hints: `let mut ways = vec![0u64; amount + 1]; ways[0] = 1;`
Outer loop over the coins, inner loop over `a` from `coin` up to `amount`.
`ways[a] += ways[a - coin];` then return `ways[amount]`.

recursion-dp-4.task:
A delivery drone flies along a street where each house offers a tip, but noise rules forbid stopping at **two neighboring houses** on the same run. Write `fn max_tips(tips: &[u32]) -> u64`: the largest total it can collect.

State: the best total using the houses up to `i`. At house `i` you either skip it (keep the best up to `i - 1`) or take it (its tip plus the best up to `i - 2`). You only ever need the last two values, so use two variables instead of a table. The tests include a street of 200,000 houses.
hints: Keep `two_back` and `one_back`, both starting at 0.
For each tip: `let best = one_back.max(two_back + tip as u64);`
Then shift: `two_back = one_back; one_back = best;`. The answer is `one_back`.

forbid.message: Keep just the last two best totals in two variables.

checkNames: may skip two in a row

recursion-dp-5.task:
A robot crosses a field from the top-left to the bottom-right cell, moving only right or down. Each cell has an energy cost, and the robot pays for every cell it visits, including the first and the last. Write `fn min_path_cost(grid: &[Vec<u32>]) -> u32`: the cheapest total (0 for an empty grid).

State: `cost[r][c]` = the cheapest way to reach cell `(r, c)`, which is the cell's own cost plus the cheaper of the cell above and the cell to the left (only one of those exists on the first row and column). The tests include a 300 by 300 field.
hints: Make `cost` the same size as the grid. The top-left cell costs just `grid[0][0]`.
First row: add the cell to the left. First column: add the cell above. Elsewhere: add the smaller of the two.
A `match (r, c)` with arms `(0, 0)`, `(0, _)`, `(_, 0)` and `_` keeps the four cases readable.
checkNames: a single row visits every cell
a single column visits every cell

recursion-dp-5.task:
Command-line tools suggest "did you mean `status`?" when you type `stauts`. They measure the **edit distance** (Levenshtein distance): the fewest single-character insertions, deletions and replacements that turn one word into the other. `kitten` to `sitting` is 3.

Write `fn edit_distance(a: &str, b: &str) -> usize` (counting characters). State: `d[i][j]` = the distance between the first `i` characters of `a` and the first `j` of `b`. Turning `i` characters into nothing takes `i` deletions (`d[i][0] = i`), and nothing into `j` characters takes `j` insertions (`d[0][j] = j`). Then if `a[i - 1] == b[j - 1]` it's `d[i - 1][j - 1]`; otherwise 1 plus the smallest of `d[i - 1][j - 1]` (replace), `d[i - 1][j]` (delete) and `d[i][j - 1]` (insert). The tests compare two 1,500-character texts.
hints: Collect both into `Vec<char>`, make the table `(a.len() + 1) x (b.len() + 1)`, and fill row 0 with `j` and column 0 with `i`.
Equal characters cost nothing: `d[i][j] = d[i - 1][j - 1]`.
Otherwise `d[i][j] = 1 + d[i - 1][j - 1].min(d[i - 1][j]).min(d[i][j - 1])`.
checkNames: empty text needs one edit per character

recursion-dp-6.task:
Two delivery vans must carry exactly the same total weight. Given the parcel weights, can they be split into two groups of equal total? Write `fn can_split_evenly(weights: &[u32]) -> bool` (no parcels: yes, two empty vans).

If the total is odd, it's impossible. Otherwise it's a knapsack question with booleans: can some subset reach exactly half the total? Keep `can[s]` for every sum `s` up to half, start with `can[0] = true`, and for each weight go through the sums **from high to low**: `can[s] = can[s] || can[s - w]`. The tests include over 100 parcels.
hints: Return `false` for an odd total. Otherwise `half = total / 2`, `let mut can = vec![false; half + 1]; can[0] = true;`
For each weight `w`, loop `s` over `(w..=half).rev()` and set `can[s] = true` when `can[s - w]` is true.
The answer is `can[half]`.
checkNames: an even total is not always enough

recursion-dp-6.task:
Now the hiker wants to know **which** items to pack. Standard input has the capacity on the first line, then one item per line: `name weight value`. Print the chosen items in input order, the total weight and the total value:

```

weight: 10/10
value: 40
```

If nothing fits, print `take: nothing`. The tests always have exactly one best choice.

Build the full 2D table from the lesson, then walk it backwards: starting at `i = n` and `w = capacity`, if `best[i][w]` differs from `best[i - 1][w]`, item `i - 1` was taken (subtract its weight from `w`). Reverse the list you collect to get input order.
hints: Parse each item line into `(name, weight, value)` and build the 2D table exactly as in the lesson's example.
Walk back with `for i in (1..=n).rev()`: when `best[i][w] != best[i - 1][w]`, item `i - 1` is in the backpack, so record it and do `w -= its weight`.
Reverse the chosen indices, join their names with `", "`, and sum their weights for the `weight:` line.

For each `(a, b)`: `following[a] += 1; followers[b] += 1;`
`(0..n).find(|&p| followers[p] == n - 1 && following[p] == 0)`

Write a maze solver. Standard input is a grid, one row per line: `S` is the start, `E` the exit, `#` a wall and `.` open floor. You can move up, down, left or right. Print `shortest path: N steps` with the fewest moves from `S` to `E`, or `no path`.

graphs-2.task:

Checking only each node against its direct children isn't enough: in the tree with root 10, left child 5 and 5's right child 12, every parent-child pair looks fine, but 12 is in 10's left subtree.
